segments.english: And I named the book The Wars of the LORD for His unity, because the philosopher, the author of the book the Zohar, spoiled for us the truth of the unity of the Name, may He be blessed, and several rabbis and great men of the Torah followed him with eyes shut. And of them Solomon said in his wisdom: "For she has cast down many slain, and mighty are all her slain." As our Rabbis of blessed memory expounded (Sanhedrin, the Rif): "For she has cast down many slain" this is a student who has not reached instruction and teaches, (as we see with our own eyes how many authors who bring an elephant through the eye of a needle, from the scantness of their expertise) "and mighty are all her slain" this is a student who has reached instruction and does not teach (who does not set his mind to teach others correctly; "mighty" is the word of "and he shuts his eyes", Rashi of blessed memory). And all the more so, if he entices others to occupy themselves with the external book, the book of the Zohar, and does not set his mind to understand the contradiction, but walks with the eye of reason shut, and makes others stumble in a false faith, of whom it is said, "and mighty are all her slain"; and transgresses against "and before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block"; and error in study counts as wilful sin, and he sins and causes the many to sin, and the sin of the many hangs on him.

tokens.note: The Tetragrammaton written as ה׳; read here as the name in the title of the book, so 'the LORD'.
הספר: 'the book'. The decisions fix 'the author of the Zohar' for מחבר הזהר; here the Hebrew has מחבר הספר הזהר, so the English keeps 'the book': 'the author of the book the Zohar'.

tokens.gloss: the Name, may He be blessed

tokens.note: רי״ף: the Rif (Rabbi Yitzchak Alfasi); the reference is kept as the author writes it, 'Sanhedrin, the Rif', with no volume or folio added.
נותן לב: idiom, literally 'gives heart': to pay attention, to set one's mind to something.

Rashi (quoted by the author at 1:5.83) connects ועצומים with the verb עוצם, 'he shuts': so 'mighty' is glossed 'he shuts his eyes', which echoes 'with eyes shut' (1:5.25-26) and 'the eye of reason shut' (1:5.102-104).
בספ׳ is the abbreviation of בספר, 'in the book of'; here the sense is 'in the book'.
ס׳ is the abbreviation of ספר.
נותן לב: the same idiom, 'gives heart': to set one's mind to understanding the contradiction.
עובר על: 'transgresses against'. על takes the cited prohibition that follows, Lev 19:14 (ולפני עור לא תתן מכשול).
A Talmudic maxim given without an introductory formula, so it takes no quotation marks.

grammar: וקראתי is a perfect with waw ('and I called'); with שם הספר it means 'named the book'.
The reason clause runs from כי (1:5.8) to בעצימת עינים (1:5.25-26): the philosopher spoiled the truth of the unity, and the followers went after him with eyes shut. From ועליהם a new sentence begins.
כי רבים חללים הפילה is Prov 7:26, said of the 'strange woman' of Prov 7 and here applied to the author of the Zohar; הפילה is a perfect, third feminine singular.
Each זה ('this is') in the Talmudic exposition introduces a rabbinic identification of one of the verse's words; the English keeps 'this is' at each point.
דמעיילי פילא בקופא דמחטא is a Talmudic Aramaic idiom for doing the impossible; the English gives its sense, 'who bring an elephant through the eye of a needle'.
ועובר על takes the cited prohibition, Lev 19:14, as its object; ושגגת תלמוד עולה זדון is a rabbinic maxim cited without a formula.
segments.note: The author's own Hebrew, with the Talmud's gloss on Prov 7:26 translated as his paraphrase. The English keeps his lists of 'this is' and 'who' clauses in order.
apparatus: The text is the Wikisource base text; Wikisource additions and corrections are not flagged word by word until the 1931 scan is collated (decisions, Q2).
The title: מלחמות ה׳ takes the form of Num 21:14, 'ספר מלחמת ה׳' (the book of the Wars of the LORD).
Prov 7:26, quoted: 'For she has cast down many slain, and mighty are all her slain' (translated from the verse as he quotes it).
Lev 19:14, 'ולפני עור לא תתן מכשול', cited after 'ועובר על': 'and before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block'.
'Sanhedrin' and 'the Rif' as written; the Talmudic gloss on the verse is his paraphrase and is not marked as a quotation.

segments.english: And concerning this external faith of the philosopher, the author of the Zohar, our Rabbis of blessed memory expounded (Yalkut, Parashat Kedoshim, and the Midrash ha-Gadol there, and the Rambam in Sefer ha-Mitzvot, negative commandment 10): "Do not turn to the idols, and the gods of; if you turn to others (to honor them, Sforno), your end is to make them divinities." Thus far. And so it befell the faith of the philosopher, the author of the Zohar, for the early students who learned from it, thinking that it was Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai the Tanna's, they thought to make sense of his words; and to call the partzufim vessels, and they esteemed them and honored them, and those who came after them made them divinities, according to the thought of the philosopher, the author, and accepted them upon themselves as divinities, as will be explained within. And likewise our Rabbis of blessed memory expounded in the verse: wine and strong drink you shall not drink, and these are his words: "Rabbi Chiya opened: 'The precepts of the LORD are right'; and it is written of wine: 'it goes down smoothly'; and it is written: 'rejoicing the heart'; and it is written: 'and wine gladdens the heart of man.' Just as this wine gladdens the heart, so the words of Torah gladden the heart; just as this wine, one who drinks of it more than his need in the end vomits everything; so the words of Torah, one who occupies himself with them and thinks about them too much, in the end he goes out into heresy." Thus far. (Midrash ha-Gadol, Parashat Shemini, verse 'wine and strong drink'). In this way did the philosopher, the false prophet, the author of the Zohar, act, to follow after his heart, to think about the words of Torah too much, in paths far from the truth, and very far from the rules that the Sages received, a man from the mouth of a man, by which the Torah is expounded, and these are the thirteen rules of Rabbi Ishmael and the thirty-three rules of Rabbi Yose the Galilean, for the Aggadah, as the discerning, attentive reader will see; and he enticed and seduced the sages, the upright of heart, who walk in their simplicity, to believe him in his lies: that there was revealed to him the Holy One, blessed be He, who is called by him the Elder of Elders, and Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, and Elijah, and they revealed to him secrets of heresy, which it is forbidden to think about them, even in the lavatory; and he promised one who occupies himself with his Torah without understanding, a reward greater than the essentials of the Torah, in order to blind the eyes of the sages and to stop up the way of study in his words so as not to understand his machinations, and to magnify the merit of those who occupy themselves with his new Torah, full of idols different in their essences and their activities, without being particular about the addition and multiplicity, in our God, the Unique, above all other ones; and do not take note how the Torah was strict about 'you shall not add', whether in tefillin, or in a mezuzah, or in the four species of the lulav, and likewise in the other commandments, even though he puts five sections in one hide and he joins them to be one, and likewise, if he adds one section to a mezuzah, even though parchment joins them to be one, we do not say 'as though it were not one'; and likewise in tzitzit, and in the bundle of four species, if he added a fifth species to the bundle, it is disqualified; and we do not say 'as though it were not one'.

tokens.note: ואלהי: construct state, 'gods of'. Lev 19:4 reads 'ואלהי מסכה'; the author's wording is cut off after ואלהי and followed by his own words, which are translated as he gives them.
ע״כ closes the quotation: 'thus far'.

רשב״י is written out in full (decisions). ל־ is possessive: the early students thought the book was Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai the Tanna's. The English does not say more than the Hebrew about who wrote it.
וז״ל introduces a quotation: 'and these are his words'.
מה ... כך: an analogy, 'just as ... so'. The Midrash sets the wine against the words of Torah.
ע״כ closes the Midrash quotation.
לתור אחרי לבבו alludes to Num 15:39, ולא תתורו אחרי לבבכם, 'and you shall not follow after your heart'.
Literally 'measures' (המדות); the hermeneutical rules by which the Torah is expounded, as the next clauses show (the thirteen rules of Rabbi Ishmael and the rules of Rabbi Yose the Galilean).
ל״ג is the letters for thirty-three, as written. The tradition counts thirty-two rules of Rabbi Yose the Galilean.

tokens.gloss: the Holy One, blessed be He

tokens.note: מגופי תורה: literally 'than the bodies of Torah'; גופי תורה are the essentials, the main body of the Torah's law.
בל תוסיף: 'you shall not add', the rabbinic name of the prohibition against adding to the commandments (Deut 4:2, 13:1), quoted by its words.
שקלף: ש + קלף, 'that parchment'. The sections are joined into one piece by the parchment, as in the tefillin case above (בעור אחד).
לחיות: the spelling in the witness for להיות, 'to be'; translated as the evident word and recorded in apparatus.
כלא חד: Aramaic, the author's halakhic formula. Rendered 'as though it were not one' (the same ruling as 1:7, which the owner will review); a possible alternative is כולא חד, 'it is all one'.

grammar: The paragraph is one long period. The quotation from Lev 19:4 (in the Yalkut, Midrash ha-Gadol and Rambam) runs from 'Do not turn' to 'Thus far'; its parenthesis is Sforno's gloss, kept in parentheses.

The Midrash ha-Gadol passage (Rabbinic Hebrew) chains verses with 'and it is written' (וכתיב): Ps 19:9, Prov 23:31 (in the Midrash's wording) and Ps 104:15. Its analogy 'just as ... so' (מה ... כך) carries the argument, and the second half turns on 'too much' (מדאי).
The infinitives after עשה (לתור, לחשב, להעור, ולסתום, ולהגדיל) give the purpose of the philosopher's deed; לתור אחרי לבבו alludes to Num 15:39, and להעור עיני חכמים to Deut 16:19.
בחשבם שהוא לרשב״י התנא: the ל of לרשב״י is possessive. The early students thought the book was Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai the Tanna's.
The verbs in the sentence about the early students (חשבו, והחשיבום, וכיבדו, עשו, וקיבלום) narrate what followed from the first error, in the perfect with waw.
דאגדתא, מינין and לא אמרינן כלא חד are Talmudic Aramaic inside the author's Hebrew; the last two clauses are the halakhic conclusion of the paragraph and the English keeps them as parallel sentences.
segments.note: One period in the Hebrew, divided at the quotation boundaries and at the Midrash's clauses. Each quotation formula is translated and each closing ע״כ is 'Thus far'.
apparatus: Lev 19:4, quoted words 'Do not turn to the idols' (אל תפנו אל האלילים). The rest of the quotation is the author's wording (ואלהי אם אתה פונה אחרים) and is rendered as he gives it; in the verse ואלהי continues 'מסכה'.
Lev 10:9, 'Wine and strong drink you shall not drink' (in the verse: wine and strong drink).
Ps 19:9: 'The precepts of the LORD are right' and 'rejoicing the heart' (משמחי לב).
Prov 23:31: 'ביין יתהלך במישרים' ('of wine: it goes down smoothly'); the verse has 'כי יתן בכוס עינו יתהלך במישרים' and the Midrash's wording is rendered as he gives it.
Ps 104:15: 'and wine gladdens the heart of man' (ויין ישמח לבב אנוש).
Num 15:39, alluded to in 'לתור אחרי לבבו' (to follow after his heart).
Deut 16:19, alluded to in 'להעור עיני חכמים' (a bribe 'blinds the eyes of the wise').
'בל תוסיף', the rabbinic name of the prohibition of Deut 4:2 and 13:1 (לא תספו / לא תסף עליו).
ל״ג in 'ול״ג מדות דר׳ יוסי הגלילי' is written as thirty-three by letters; the English follows the wave 1 ruling (thirty-three). The usual count of Rabbi Yose the Galilean's rules is thirty-two.
לחיות (1:6.307) is the witness's spelling of להיות; translated 'to be'.
כלא חד (1:6.311, 1:6.326): rendered 'as though it were not one' under the owner's reservation on 1:7; a possible alternative reading is כולא חד, 'it is all one'.
